body.text: Since the February 2025 inauguration of the second Trump administration, New Delhi has struggled to find a way to deal with the constantly swinging moods in Washington. Although the still-emerging strategic partnership between the two has, at times, seemed to take center stage, on most occasions, U.S. President Donald Trump appears to have expressed very little affinity for India, his vice president’s matrimonial ties to the country notwithstanding.

The tariffs imposed on India – at one time among the highest for targeted countries – and the failure to arrive at a trade deal despite prolonged negotiations are among the many irritants that have seeped into the relationship.

Beyond all else, there is the stark reality that in Washington’s calculations India appears to matter only to the extent it episodically can be played off against China. In this context, U.S. Secretary of State Mark Rubio’s two-day visit to India on October 20-21 may not have provided the positive breakthrough New Delhi was earnestly looking for, highlighting instead the contours of the changing strategic partnership and the increasingly erratic nature of U.S. foreign policy under Trump 2.0.

Rubio broke a protocol of sorts. His first stop was Mumbai, India’s financial capital. As a result, there was no meeting between him and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, which would have been a foregone conclusion had he included New Delhi in his itinerary. In Mumbai, he met the top two industrial chiefs of the country: Gautam Adani of the Adani Group and N. Chandrasekharan of the Tata Group. India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, who recently aired his grievances against the U.S., flew down to Mumbai to meet Rubio as well as visiting UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed.

That the U.S. secretary of state could decide the venue of his meeting with his Indian counterpart while in India has been criticized by the opposition parties. It also dovetails squarely with emerging assessment that U.S. strategy is divorced from any cogent calculations, responding rather to rapidly shifting whims and fancies of a transactional leader.

Following the meetings – bilaterally between Jaishankar and Rubio, another between Jaishankar and bin Zayed and finally, all three together – a readout of cooperation was issued. Curiously missing were two important initiatives involving all three countries: the I2U2 and the India-Middle East Economic Corridor (IMEC).

The I2U2 was formed by the three countries along with Israel in 2021, and the IMEC was announced in 2023. Both projects have stalled due to a variety of reasons including the war in Iran. Jaishankar’s summation of the trilateral meeting as a “useful exchange of perspectives on energy, connectivity and contemporary developments” was a clear indicator of the limited outcome of the confabulation and served only to raise questions concerning U.S. intentions.

Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor did try to sound optimistic while predicting the future of the India-U.S. trade deal. Rubio said that the deal, which is allegedly 99 percent complete, could be only “weeks away” from being signed. This kind of temporal signaling is de rigor in Trump administration communications, but generally has little connection to real time. Rubio, in fact, uttered those same words on June 4 while testifying before the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee. “We can wrap up the negotiations on our trade agreement, which we think we’re a few weeks away from being able to conclude,” he said roughly 20 weeks ago.

The latest statement of reassurance comes amid pessimistic Indian assessments, including that of the country’s finance minister. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting on October 5, Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said, “The negotiations are still ongoing but we would like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult.” Trump’s October 20 prediction about a “much different” trade deal with India hasn’t cleared the air of the ambivalence surrounding the future of the deal.

Rubio’s second and final stop was Jamnagar in the western Indian state of Gujarat, to visit the refinery of Reliance Industries to discuss energy cooperation and push for Indian imports of heavy Venezuelan crude. The latter may point to the true heart of the visit: seeking a way to involve India in transactional U.S. foreign policy by offering select Indian players a chance to profit from the questionable finances of ventures such as those in Venezuela. Jamnagar, which possesses the specialized high-capacity infrastructure required to process thick and high-sulfur heavy Venezuelan crude, is also the world’s largest single-location refining complex. A further tradeoff from the trip thus could also be to provide Rubio with a reason to claim, just before the impending U.S. mid-terms, that there is impending relief from high domestic diesel and energy prices.

Reliance Industries, led by Mukesh Ambani, is also embracing the prospect of such closer cooperation. Rubio and his wife were welcomed by the entire Ambani family, consisting of Mukesh’s wife, his sons, daughters, and their spouses. Apart from touring the oil-refining complex and Reliance’s emerging clean-energy manufacturing hub, Rubio also visited the Vantara, a controversial wildlife rescue and conservation center curated and led by one of Mukesh Ambani’s sons.

Although Rubio explained his trip as a measure to strengthen bilateral trade ties, the thrust of the trip seems more focused on American domestic politics, a search for mid-term talking points by courting new buyers and markets for expanded Venezuelan oil production. The opaque finances of the entire Venezuelan escapade notwithstanding – it has been widely reported that there has been no public accounting of just where Venezuelan oil profits are going – Reliance Industries is also planning investment in a new refinery in Texas, which Gor tweeted is “an opportunity to expand U.S. energy production and create jobs.”

Indeed, during the visit, Rubio termed India the “refining superpower of the world.” This was music to select Indian media, owned by Reliance Industries, which doubled down on the point that India, which imports 89 percent of its energy requirements from different countries, is the fourth largest exporter of refined petroleum products.

What India stands to gain out of the possible deal between Reliance Industries and the United States isn’t clear. Who will bear the cost if U.S. policies shift again remains an unanswered question. Given the fact that the U.S. is now importing Russian diesel against the will of the U.S. Congress – with its composition up for grabs in a matter of weeks – that would seem to raise questions concerning the rationale behind putting New Delhi’s import of Russian crude under permanent scanner and possible sanctions.

For decades, India has treated strategic, defense, and technology cooperation as the core of its partnership with the United States. But under Trump 2.0, the relationship is being recast as a transaction built on trade and energy, with India now viewed as buyer, refiner, and market. Rubio’s itinerary, which skipped the corridors of power for boardrooms and a refinery, made the point amply clear. Whether dancing to the American tune is a prudent strategy for India remains to be seen as transactionalism is gradually eroding what could have been the defining strategic partnership of the 21st century.
